title: Art, Culture, and Festivals of Assam

blocks.content: Covers Assam's rich cultural heritage — festivals, performing arts, and the neo-Vaishnavite movement — a colourful, high-yield area consistently tested across all Assam GS papers.

items: Bihu is celebrated three times a year, marking different points in the agricultural cycle — Rongali/Bohag Bihu (mid-April, marks the Assamese New Year and the onset of the sowing season, the most widely celebrated of the three), Kongali/Kati Bihu (mid-October, a more austere observance associated with the lean agricultural period), and Bhogali/Magh Bihu (mid-January, a harvest festival marked by feasting and community bonfires called 'Meji').

Bihu dance — a energetic folk dance performed by young men and women during Rongali Bihu, characterized by brisk steps, distinctive hand gestures, and traditional attire; typically accompanied by instruments including the dhol (drum), pepa (buffalo-horn pipe), and taal (cymbals).

Bihu has been recognized with cultural significance at national and international levels, including efforts toward UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage recognition, reflecting its importance to Assamese identity.
The neo-Vaishnavite (Ek Sarana Naam Dharma) movement was founded by Srimanta Sankardev in the 15th–16th century, profoundly shaping Assamese religious, literary, and artistic traditions.

Sankardev is credited with founding the institution of the Satra (a monastery-cum-cultural-institution) and contributing extensively to Assamese literature, music (Borgeet), and dance-drama (Ankiya Naat/Bhaona).
Majuli, the river island in the Brahmaputra, is the historical epicentre of satra culture, hosting numerous satras that continue to preserve and transmit these traditions.

Sattriya dance, one of the eight classical dance forms officially recognized by the Sangeet Natak Akademi, originated within this satra tradition and remains closely associated with Assamese Vaishnavite religious practice.

Kamakhya Temple, located on Nilachal Hill near Guwahati, is one of the most significant Shakti Peethas in Hindu tradition and a major centre of Tantric worship; the annual Ambubachi Mela held here draws large numbers of pilgrims.

Assam is home to substantial ethnic and religious diversity, including numerous indigenous tribal communities (such as the Bodo, Karbi, Mising, Rabha, and many others), each with distinct festivals, languages, and cultural practices that regularly feature in GS questions.

Traditional Assamese cuisine, characterized by an emphasis on rice, fish, and minimal use of heavy spices, along with distinctive items like khar (an alkaline preparation) and various fermented foods, is occasionally tested in cultural-GK sections.

cells:
Exam Tip

• The three Bihu festivals, their approximate timing, and their agricultural significance is one of the most heavily and consistently tested topics in all of Assam GS — memorize all three precisely, not just Rongali Bihu.

• Srimanta Sankardev's contributions (Satra institution, Sattriya dance, Borgeet, Ankiya Naat) are frequently tested both individually and as a linked set.

• Sattriya dance's status as one of the eight classical dance forms of India (alongside Bharatanatyam, Kathak, etc.) is a frequently repeated cross-subject GK fact.
